syllabus.clause: task retry up to spark.task.maxFailures; fetch failures that resubmit the parent shuffle-map stage; executor loss taking shuffle files with it (external shuffle service, graceful decommissioning with block migration on Kubernetes); speculative execution and its hazard with non-idempotent sinks.

at.step: Reveal: the baseline -- given enough tries, the job finishes
Reveal: it gives up -- the job aborts this time
Elaborate: why -- a retry limit is a fixed number of chances
Reveal: far more -- the entire earlier stage reruns
Elaborate: why -- there's no partial fix available

items.item: speculative execution re-launches a slow task as a second, independent attempt alongside the original
graceful decommissioning migrates both RDD blocks and shuffle blocks to a remote executor before the executor shuts down
Kubernetes has its own decommissioning script hook, and an external shuffle service is not yet available on Kubernetes at this Spark version

A non-idempotent sink (an append, an external counter increment, a non-transactional write) is genuinely unsafe under speculation specifically because both the original and the speculative copy of a task can perform that side effect independently -- unlike an idempotent sink (an overwrite, a deduplicated upsert), where either copy winning the race produces the same final result.

at.out: the non-idempotent-vs-idempotent sink distinction named only; this topic's own examples.py measures task retry and fetch-failure stage resubmission, not a live speculative double-write

items.item: spark.speculation.quantile (default 0.9) and spark.speculation.multiplier (default 3) together gate when speculation actually triggers -- most tasks in a stage must already be done, and a straggler must be several times slower than the already-finished median, before Spark considers launching a speculative copy at all, which is why a small or evenly-paced job may never speculate even with speculation enabled.

at.out: the quantile/multiplier gating thresholds named only; this topic's own examples.py does not reproduce a live speculative relaunch, since this sandbox's own scheduler did not reliably trigger one across repeated attempts

items.item: spark.excludeOnFailure (the health tracker referenced directly in TaskSetManager's own fetch-failure handling) can exclude the executor or node that produced a fetch failure from receiving further tasks, a separate mitigation from the stage resubmission this topic's own examples.py measures -- excluding a bad node and resubmitting the stage are two different responses to the same fetch failure.

at.out: the health tracker's own executor/node exclusion on fetch failure named only; this topic's own examples.py measures the stage resubmission itself, not the exclusion mechanism

items.item: The external shuffle service, where available (YARN, standalone with the service enabled), lets a reduce task keep reading an executor's shuffle output even after that executor process has exited -- the specific mechanism this topic's own sourced Kubernetes page admits isn't yet available there, which is exactly why graceful decommissioning's own block migration matters more on Kubernetes than on a cluster manager that does offer the service.

at.out: the external shuffle service's own role on YARN/standalone named only, contrasting with Kubernetes's own lack of it (sourced directly); this topic's own examples.py reproduces a fetch failure via direct file deletion in local mode, which has neither mechanism

items.item: spark.executor.decommission.killInterval and spark.executor.decommission.forceKillTimeout bound how long Spark waits for block migration to finish before forcibly killing a decommissioning executor anyway -- naming the real time pressure graceful decommissioning operates under, distinct from this topic's own measured claims about ordinary task retry and fetch failure.

at.out: the decommission timeout configs named only; this topic's own examples.py does not exercise decommissioning directly

items.item: spark.speculation.task.duration.threshold exists specifically because the ordinary quantile/multiplier gating fails on a stage with very few tasks (too few for a meaningful median) -- a special-case speculation trigger based on an absolute duration rather than a relative one, which is also likely why this topic's own small-scale speculation probes (8-32 tasks) never triggered a relaunch under the ordinary gating alone.

at.out: the duration-threshold special case for small stages named only, as the likely reason this topic's own probes could not reliably reproduce a live speculative relaunch; this topic's own examples.py does not set this config

items.item: A task retry (within maxTaskFailures) and a stage resubmission (from a fetch failure) show up differently in an event log: a retry is a new task attempt within the same stage attempt, while a fetch-failure resubmission is an entirely new stage attempt containing new attempts of every task in that stage -- the exact distinction this topic's own outcome (tracing an event log) is built around.

at.out: the event-log-level distinction between a task retry and a stage resubmission named explicitly, directly matching this topic's own stated learning outcome; this topic's own examples.py confirms the distinction via the REST API's stage-attempt structure rather than parsing a raw event log file

items.item: spark.speculation.efficiency.enabled and its related configs (processRateMultiplier, longRunTaskFactor), added in Spark 3.4, refine naive speculation by checking whether a slow task's low *data processing rate* (not just its wall-clock duration) justifies a speculative copy -- avoiding wasted speculative relaunches of tasks that are merely handling more data, not actually stuck.

at.out: speculation efficiency's own data-rate-aware refinement named only; this topic's own examples.py does not exercise this refinement

items.item: dynamic allocation on Kubernetes requires spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled specifically because Kubernetes doesn't support an external shuffle service, the same gap this topic's own sourced Kubernetes page names directly -- without shuffle tracking, Spark could remove an executor that's still holding shuffle data other tasks need.

at.out: shuffle tracking as Kubernetes's own workaround for lacking an external shuffle service named only, cross-referencing this topic's own sourced admission; this topic's own examples.py does not exercise dynamic allocation

items.item: spark.kubernetes.executor.missingPodDetectDelta is a distinct failure-detection path from a fetch failure or a GC-induced heartbeat timeout: it's the delay Kubernetes-specific pod-polling uses before concluding an executor's own pod is simply gone from the cluster, rather than merely slow or unresponsive -- a third way an executor's loss gets detected, beyond the heartbeat-timeout path the previous topic named.

at.out: pod-polling-based executor-loss detection on Kubernetes named only, as a third detection path distinct from the previous topic's own heartbeat-timeout path; this topic's own examples.py does not run on Kubernetes
